newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Hopes for budget cut weigh on Israeli shekel.
newsitem.headline: Hopes for budget cut weigh on Israeli shekel.

text.p: The Israeli currency market has bid up the dollar by 1.1 percent this week on a bet the government will cut 1997 spending and it may take it higher once the budget is approved, dealers said on Wednesday.
"The market is working on a no-alternative assumption, that (the budget) has to go through," said Ilan Raviv, manager of the currency dealing room at Israel Discount Bank.

Israel's parliament is being asked to cut as much as seven billion shekels from next year's budget. If the seven billion shekels, or a figure close to it, is approved, dealers said the Bank of Israel would move quickly to lower the base short-term rate from the current 15.2 percent.

An interest rate cut would alleviate much of the upward pressure on the shekel that has developed as a result of capital imports by Israeli companies taking advantage of cheaper foreign currency loans.
"If there is a seven billion shekel cut, the dollar will jump, but I'm pessimistic," said Ilan Zadka, a dealer at United Mizrahi Bank.

The Treasury's proposed spending cuts have met wide opposition in parliament, even among coalition legislators. Therefore, Zadka said, it was more realistic to expect that parliament would approve a cut of 5.5-6 billion shekels.

But even a smaller spending cut, he said, would prompt the Bank of Israel to cut the base rate 1-1.5 percentage points. If so, he said the dollar could reach as high as 3.37 shekels. If the full seven billion shekel cut is approved, the dollar could even reach 3.40, he added.
The dollar representative rate was fixed at 3.29 shekels on Wednesday, after trading as high as 3.3005 during trading.

Dealers said they were not sure when the central bank would move. Parliament has until December 31 to pass the budget, but the Bank of Israel is scheduled to announce its January monetary programme, including interest rates, December 23.
Zadka said he doubted the bank would make a significant cut in December, but did not rule out the possibility that it might announce a reduction in early January.
Raviv said 3.30 shekels was the near-term ceiling for the U.S. currency. "The market sees 3.30 as a pivot level, because we've been there before and we never broke it," he said.
"If we break through 3.30, we'll see a lot of momentum on the upside," he added.

Ilan Viskin, currency trading manager at Bank Hapoalim, said he was not convinced the market was being influenced by budget considerations. He attributed most of this week's dollar gains to a rising dollar worldwide.
Viskin noted that the rate for the currency basket, to which the shekel is officially tied, had not moved as much as the dollar rate. The basket has gained only 0.6 percent since Friday.
